checking for a local model…
Type anything. If it is not in the bank word for word it is matched to the nearest question, and the answer comes with what they do as well as what they say. They are allowed to lie to you — and the thing that catches them out is always a test, never a hunch.
LOOK AT THEM
Click a part of the body to look at it. Click it again to look properly — some things only show up when you do, and nothing here will tell you what it means.
THE NEEDLE
Whether you get it depends on the veins in front of you, and they depend on the patient. Go through the back wall and it blows; go deep in the fossa and you will find the artery or the nerve. Each attempt costs them something.

Nothing here is medicine, and none of it is decoration. The room is measured — light, noise, heat, the bed, your hands — and what is kind depends on what is wrong with them. A tick means it is already like that.

CALL SURGERY — ask for anything you like
They will ask what you have to justify it, whether the patient is fit to be induced, and whether anyone has consented them. They are allowed to say no.
SIGN THEM OFF
Write what you think it is and decide where they go. Nothing here tells you whether you were right. You find that out from what happens to them afterwards — and if you were wrong, they come back.
HAND THEM OVER
Refer them on, using the diagnosis in the box above. They will not take a patient without one, and if the name does not fit the numbers you are reading out they will say so. If they accept it, they treat what you told them — and if you were wrong, they ring you back.
NEWS —
Nothing to debrief yet. It appears once you have signed them off and found out what happened.

Nothing here is guarded. The dose you type is the dose that is given, the drug goes in even if it is the one they are allergic to, and the operation happens if the surgeon agrees to it. Diagnoses are dealt at their real prevalence — mostly ordinary, occasionally not. You are never told which one you got.

Everything starts textbook normal — 72 bpm, 120/80, 98%, 16/min, etCO2 38, 98.6°F. The rate is not a fixed number with jitter painted on: each R–R interval shortens on inspiration and lengthens on expiration (respiratory sinus arrhythmia) with a little noise on top, and the displayed value averages the last four intervals — so it wanders 69–75 the way a real patient does. Every pleth pulse is the beat that caused it, one sweep behind, and the beep pitch falls as SpO2 drops.

Matching TruMonitor's sound is yours to finish — I can't hear audio, so I can't copy it by ear. What makes a tone read as a ting is the envelope, not the pitch: a decaying tone rings like a struck bell, so these are gated instead — up, hold flat, stop. Beep (square) is the default; Ting (old) is kept only so you can hear the difference. Length is the one that makes a beep sound slower — echo is off by default and is a separate thing. Master warning is three beeps; the minor alarm is two at the same pace, pitched lower. Charge & shock runs the defibrillator: capacitor whine, discharge, and a shockable rhythm converts — try it from VFib.
